According to the Society's statement to the newspaper, its incoming president [[Sir Paul Nurse]] had written to Musk, asking him to consider resigning his fellowship if he felt unable to promote or support science. The Society told the ''FT'' that Musk did not respond on that point and that staff concluded it was not in the Society's interests to pursue disciplinary action.{{cite news |last=Ahuja |first=Anjana |author-link=Anjana Ahuja |date=October 2025 |title=The Royal Society should be protecting science, not Musk |url=https://www.ft.com/content/d4eb987a-a3df-4c81-8675-d4005bd6c1b7 |access-date=8 October 2025 |work=[[Financial Times]] |type=Opinion}} ==Coat of arms== [[File:Arms of the Royal Society.svg|thumb|right|upright|Detail of the [[Escutcheon (heraldry)|escutcheon]] of the Royal Society's arms]] The blazon for the [[coat of arms]] of the Royal Society is ''in a dexter corner of a shield argent our three Lions of England, and for crest a helm adorned with a crown studded with florets, surmounted by an eagle of proper colour holding in one foot a shield charged with our lions: supporters two white hounds gorged with crowns'', with the motto of ''[[nullius in verba]]''. John Evelyn, interested in the early structure of the society, had sketched out at least six possible designs, but in August 1662 [[Charles II of England|Charles II]] told the society that it was allowed to use the arms of England as part of its coat and the society "now resolv'd that the armes of the Society should be, ''a field Argent, with a canton of the armes of England; the supporters two talbots Argent''; Crest, ''an eagle Or holding a shield with the like armes of England, viz. 3 lions''. The words ''Nullius in verba''". This was approved by Charles, who asked [[Garter King of Arms]] to create a diploma for it, and when the second charter was signed on 22 April 1663 the arms were granted to the president, council and fellows of the society along with their successors.J.D.G.D. (1938) p.37 The helmet of the arms was not specified in the charter, but the engraver sketched out a [[Helmet (heraldry)#United Kingdom|peer's helmet]] (barred helmet) on the final design, which is used. This is contrary to the heraldic rules, as a society or corporation normally has an esquire's helmet (closed helmet); it is thought that either the engraver was ignorant of this rule, which was not strictly adhered to until around 1615, or that he used the peer's helmet as a compliment to [[William Brouncker, 2nd Viscount Brouncker|Lord Brouncker]], a peer and the first President of the Royal Society.J.D.G.D. (1938) p.38 == Charter book == Fellows and foreign members are required to sign a book when they join the Royal Society. This book is known as the Charter Book, which has been signed continuously since 1663. All British monarchs have signed the book since then, apart from William and Mary, and Queen Anne.{{Cite web |title=Turning a new page in the Charter Book |date=8 July 2019 |first1=Louisiane |last1=Ferlier |url=https://royalsociety.org/blog/2019/07/turning-a-new-page-in-the-charter-book/ |access-date=2023-08-02 |website=Royal Society |archive-date=7 June 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230607031755/https://royalsociety.org/blog/2019/07/turning-a-new-page-in-the-charter-book/ |url-status=live }} In 2019, the book was digitised. ==Motto== The society's motto, ''[[Nullius in verba]]'', is [[Latin]] for "Take nobody's word for it". It was adopted to signify the fellows' determination to establish facts via experiments and comes from [[Horace]]'s ''[[Epistles (Horace)|Epistles]]'', where he compares himself to a [[gladiator]] who, having retired, is free from control.{{cite web |url=https://royalsociety.org/about-us/history/ |title=History |publisher=The Royal Society |access-date=29 October 2015 |archive-date=19 May 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200519184323/https://royalsociety.org/about-us/history/ |url-status=live }} ==Fellows of the Royal Society (FRS)== {{main|Fellow of the Royal Society|List of Fellows of the Royal Society|List of female Fellows of the Royal Society}} [[File:J.J Thomson.jpg|right|thumb|upright|[[J. J. Thomson]] was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1884.]] The society's core members are the fellows: scientists and engineers from the United Kingdom and the Commonwealth selected based on having made "a substantial contribution to the improvement of natural knowledge, including mathematics, engineering science and medical science".{{cite web |url=http://royalsociety.org/Criteria-for-candidates/ |title=Criteria for candidates |publisher=The Royal Society |access-date=5 December 2009 |archive-date=7 December 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091207124145/http://royalsociety.org/Criteria-for-candidates/ |url-status=dead }} Fellows are elected for life and gain the right to use the [[Post-nominal letters|postnominal]] [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] (FRS). The rights and responsibilities of fellows also include a duty to financially contribute to the society, the right to stand for council posts and the right to elect new fellows.{{cite web |url=http://royalsociety.org/rights-and-responsibilities/ |title=The rights and responsibilities of Fellows of the Royal Society |publisher=The Royal Society |access-date=5 December 2009 |archive-date=7 December 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091207124239/http://royalsociety.org/rights-and-responsibilities/ |url-status=dead }} Up to 52 fellows are elected each year and in 2014 there were about 1,450 living members in total.{{cite web |url=http://royalsociety.org/Fellows/ |title=Fellows |publisher=The Royal Society |access-date=24 March 2014 |archive-date=5 September 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150905100644/https://royalsociety.org/fellows/ |url-status=dead }} Election to the fellowship is decided by ten sectional committees (each covering a subject area or set of subjects areas) which consist of existing fellows. The society also elects royal fellows, honorary fellows and foreign members. Royal fellows are those members of the [[British royal family]], representing the [[Monarchy of the United Kingdom|British monarchy]]'s role in promoting and supporting the society, who are recommended by the society's council and elected via postal vote. There are currently four royal fellows: [[Charles III|The King of the United Kingdom]], [[Prince Edward, Duke of Kent|The Duke of Kent]], [[Anne, Princess Royal|The Princess Royal]], and [[William, Prince of Wales|The Prince of Wales]]. Honorary fellows are people who are ineligible to be elected as fellows but nevertheless have "rendered signal service to the cause of science, or whose election would significantly benefit the Society by their great experience in other walks of life". Six honorary fellows have been elected to date, including [[Onora O'Neill, Baroness O'Neill of Bengarve|Baroness O'Neill of Bengarve]].{{cite web |url=http://royalsociety.org/Honorary-Fellows/ |title=Honorary Fellows |publisher=The Royal Society |access-date=5 December 2009 |archive-date=7 December 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091207124540/http://royalsociety.org/Honorary-Fellows/ |url-status=dead }} Foreign members are scientists from non-Commonwealth nations "who are eminent for their scientific discoveries and attainments". Eight are elected each year by the society and also hold their membership for life. Foreign members are permitted to use the post-nominal ForMemRS (Foreign Member of the Royal Society) and as of August 2020 number about 185.{{cite web |url=http://royalsociety.org/about-us/fellowship/foreign-members/ |title=Foreign Members |publisher=The Royal Society |access-date=16 May 2013 |archive-date=27 September 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100927085642/http://royalsociety.org/about-us/fellowship/foreign-members/ |url-status=dead }} [[File:Stephen_Hawking.StarChild.jpg|right|thumb|upright|[[Stephen Hawking]] was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1974.]] The appointment of fellows was first authorised in the second charter, issued on 22 April 1663, which allowed the president and council, in the two months following the signing, to appoint as fellows any individual they saw fit. This saw the appointment of 94 fellows on 20 May and 4 on 22 June; these 98 are known as the "Original Fellows". After the expiration of this two-month period, any appointments were to be made by the president, council and existing fellows.de Beer (1950) p.172 Many early fellows were not scientists or particularly eminent intellectuals; it was clear that the early society could not rely on financial assistance from the king, and scientifically trained fellows were few and far between. It was, therefore, necessary to secure the favour of wealthy or important individuals for the society's survival.Lyons (1939) p.109 While the entrance fee of £4 and the subscription rate of one [[shilling]] a week should have produced £600 a year for the society, many fellows paid neither regularly nor on time.Lyons (1939) p.110 Two-thirds of the fellows in 1663 were non-scientists; this rose to 71.6% in 1800 before dropping to 47.4% in 1860 as the financial security of the society became more certain.Lyons (1939) p.112 In May 1846, a committee recommended limiting the annual intake of members to 15 and insisting on scientific eminence; this was implemented, with the result being that the society now consists exclusively of scientific fellows.Lyons (1938) p.45 ==Structure and governance== The society is governed by its council, which is chaired by the society's [[List of Presidents of the Royal Society|president]], according to a set of statutes and standing orders. The members of council, the president, and the other officers are elected from and by its fellowship. ===Council=== The council is a body consisting of 20 to 24 fellows,{{cite web |title=Statutes of the Royal Society |url=https://royalsociety.org/~/media/about-us/governance/royal-society-statutes-290115.pdf |publisher=The Royal Society |access-date=9 March 2023 |archive-date=7 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230307155827/https://royalsociety.org/~/media/about-us/governance/royal-society-statutes-290115.pdf |url-status=live }} including the officers (the president, the treasurer, two secretaries—one from the physical sciences, one from life sciences—and the foreign secretary),{{cite web |last1=Poliakoff |first1=Martyn |title=The Royal Society, the Foreign Secretary, and International Relations |url=http://www.sciencediplomacy.org/letter-field/2015/royal-society-foreign-secretary-and-international-relations |website=sciencediplomacy.org |publisher=Science & Diplomacy |access-date=24 March 2015 |archive-date=16 May 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190516191053/http://www.sciencediplomacy.org/letter-field/2015/royal-society-foreign-secretary-and-international-relations |url-status=dead }} one fellow to represent each sectional committee and seven other fellows.{{cite web |url=http://www2.royalsociety.org/page.asp?id=1026 |title=How is the Society governed? |publisher=The Royal Society |access-date=6 December 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080609015141/http://royalsociety.org/page.asp?id=1026 |archive-date=9 June 2008}} The council is tasked with directing the society's overall policy, managing all business related to the society, amending, making or repealing the society's standing orders and acting as trustees for the society's possessions and estates. Members are elected annually via a postal ballot, and current standing orders mean that at least ten seats must change hands each year.{{cite web |url=http://www2.royalsociety.org/page.asp?id=2233 |title=The Council |publisher=The Royal Society |access-date=6 December 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080609051042/http://royalsociety.org/page.asp?id=2233 |archive-date=9 June 2008}} The council may establish (and is assisted by) a variety of committees, which can include not only fellows but also outside scientists. Under the charter, the president, two secretaries and the treasurer are collectively the officers of the society.Lyons (1940) p. 115 The current officers{{cite web |title=Council |url=https://royalsociety.org/about-us/committees/council-37/ |website=The Royal Society |access-date=2 December 2020 |archive-date=12 November 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201112110737/https://royalsociety.org/about-us/committees/council-37/ |url-status=live }} are: * President: [[Sir Paul Nurse]] * Treasurer: [[Jonathan Keating]] * Biological Secretary: [[Sir David Baulcombe]] * Physical Secretary: [[Sheila Rowan (physicist)|Sheila Rowan]] * Foreign Secretary: [[Sir Mark Walport]] and [[Alison Noble]] (jointly) ===President=== {{main|List of presidents of the Royal Society}} The president of the Royal Society is the head of both the society and the council. The details for the presidency were set out in the second charter and initially had no limit on how long a president could serve; under current society statute, the term is five years.{{cite web |url=https://royalsociety.org/blog/2015/08/misogallus-on-the-warpath/ |title=Misogallus on the warpath |publisher=The Royal Society |access-date=2 December 2020 |archive-date=27 October 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201027091628/https://royalsociety.org/blog/2015/08/misogallus-on-the-warpath/ |url-status=live }} The current president is [[Sir Paul Nurse]], who took over from [[Adrian Smith (statistician)|Adrian Smith]] on 1 December 2025.{{Cite web |title=Paul Nurse elected as next President of the Royal Society {{!}} Royal Society |url=https://royalsociety.org/news/2024/10/paul-nurse-next-president-royal-society/ |access-date=2026-02-08 |website=royalsociety.org |language=en}} Historically, the duties of the president have been both formal and social. The [[Cruelty to Animals Act, 1876]] left the president as one of the few individuals capable of certifying that a particular experiment on an animal was justified. In addition, the president is to act as the government's chief (albeit informal) advisor on scientific matters. Yet another task is that of entertaining distinguished foreign guests and scientists.{{cite journal |year=1885 |title=The Presidency of the Royal Society of London |url=https://archive.org/details/sim_science_1885-11-20_6_146/page/442 |journal=Science |volume=6 |issue=146 |doi=10.1126/science.ns-6.146.442 |pmid=17749567 |bibcode=1885Sci.....6..442. |pages=442–3}} ===Permanent staff=== The society is assisted by a number of full-time paid staff. The original charter provided for "two or more Operators of Experiments, and two or more clerks"; as the number of books in the society's collection grew, it also became necessary to employ a curator. The staff grew as the financial position of the society improved, mainly consisting of outsiders, along with a small number of scientists who were required to resign their fellowship on employment.Robinson (1946) p.193 The current executive director is [[Julie Maxton|Dame Julie Maxton DBE]].{{cite web |url=https://royalsociety.org/about-us/governance/staff/ |title=Staff |publisher=The Royal Society |access-date=1 October 2017 |archive-date=1 October 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171001212911/https://royalsociety.org/about-us/governance/staff/ |url-status=live }} ==Functions and activities== [[File:The Royal Society - Senate House History Day 2019.jpg|thumb|The Royal Society Collections at the University of London History Day, 2019]] The society has a variety of functions and activities. It supports modern science by disbursing over £100 million to fund almost 1,000 research fellowships for both early and late-career scientists, along with innovation, mobility and research capacity grants.{{cite web |url=https://royalsociety.org/grants/ |title=Grants |publisher=The Royal Society |access-date=28 October 2014 |archive-date=9 October 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141009213258/https://royalsociety.org/grants/ |url-status=live }} Its [[Awards, lectures and medals of the Royal Society|awards, prize lectures and medals]] all come with prize money intended to finance research,{{cite web |url=http://royalsociety.org/Awards/ |title=Awards, medals and prize lectures |publisher=The Royal Society |access-date=7 December 2009 |archive-date=15 June 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130615004534/http://royalsociety.org/awards/ |url-status=live }} and it provides subsidised communications and media skills courses for research scientists.{{cite web |url=http://royalsociety.org/Communication-and-Media-Training/ |title=Communication skills and Media training courses |publisher=The Royal Society |access-date=7 December 2009 |archive-date=3 December 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091203165431/http://royalsociety.org/Communication-and-Media-Training/ |url-status=live }} Much of this activity is supported by a grant from the [[Department for Business, Innovation and Skills]], most of which is channelled to the [[Royal Society University Research Fellowship|University Research Fellowships (URF)]]. In 2008, the society opened the Royal Society Enterprise Fund, intended to invest in new scientific companies and be self-sustaining, funded (after an initial set of donations on the 350th anniversary of the society) by the returns from its investments.{{cite web |url=http://www2.royalsociety.org/enterprisefund/index.htm |title=The Royal Society Enterprise Fund |publisher=The Royal Society Enterprise Fund |access-date=7 December 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100619082943/http://royalsociety.org/enterprisefund/index.htm |archive-date=19 June 2010 }} Through its Science Policy Centre, the society acts as an advisor to the [[Government of the United Kingdom|UK Government]], the [[European Commission]] and the [[United Nations]] on matters of science. It publishes several reports a year, and serves as the [[Academy of Sciences]] of the United Kingdom.{{cite book |title=Science Policy Centre – 2010 and beyond |publisher=The Royal Society |year=2009 |page=3}} Since the middle of the 18th century, government problems involving science were irregularly referred to the society, and by 1800 it was done regularly.Hall (1981) p.629 ==Carlton House Terrace== [[File:Royal Society 20040420.jpg|thumb|The current premises of the Royal Society, 6–9 [[Carlton House Terrace]], London (first four properties only)]] The premises at 6–9 [[Carlton House Terrace]] is a Grade I listed building and the current headquarters of the Royal Society, which had moved there from [[Burlington House]] in 1967.{{cite web |url=http://royalsociety.org/History-of-the-Royal-Society/ |title=General |publisher=The Royal Society |access-date=7 December 2009 |archive-date=18 December 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091218075650/http://royalsociety.org/History-of-the-Royal-Society/ |url-status=live }} The ground floor and basement are used for ceremonies, social and publicity events, the first floor hosts facilities for Fellows and Officers of the society, and the second and third floors are divided between offices and accommodation for the President, Executive Director and Fellows.Fischer (2005) p.66 Carlton House Terrace was designed by [[John Nash (architect)|John Nash]] as two blocks of houses, with a space in between them.Summerson (1967) p.20 The building is still owned by the [[Crown Estates]] and leased by the society; it underwent a major renovation from 2001 to 2004 at the cost of £9.8 million, and was reopened by [[Charles, Prince of Wales|the Prince of Wales]] on 7 July 2004. Carlton House Terrace underwent a series of renovations between 1999 and November 2003 to improve and standardise the property. New waiting, exhibition and reception rooms were created in the house at No.7, using the Magna Boschi marble found in No.8, and greenish grey Statuario Venato marble was used in other areas to standardise the design. An effort was also made to make the layout of the buildings easier, consolidating all the offices on one floor, Fellows' Rooms on another and all the accommodation on a third.Fischer (2005) p.67 ==Kavli Royal Society International Centre== In 2009 [[Chicheley Hall]], a Grade I listed building located near [[Milton Keynes]], was bought by the Royal Society for £6.5 million, funded in part by the [[Kavli Foundation (United States)|Kavli Foundation]].{{cite web |url=http://www.timesonline.co.uk/tol/news/uk/science/article5993113.ece |title="Royal Society snaps up a stately hothouse", Times Online, 29 March 2009 |publisher=Timesonline.co.uk |access-date=17 August 2012 |archive-date=12 November 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231112152353/https://www.thetimes.co.uk/ |url-status=dead }} The Royal Society spent several million on renovations adapting it to become the Kavli Royal Society International Centre, a venue for residential science seminars. ''[[Notes and Records]]'' is the society's journal of the history of science.{{cite web |url=http://rsnr.royalsocietypublishing.org/site/misc/about.xhtml |title=About Notes and Records |publisher=The Royal Society |access-date=11 December 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120719031921/http://rsnr.royalsocietypublishing.org/site/misc/about.xhtml |archive-date=19 July 2012 }} [[Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society|''Biographical Memoirs'']] is published twice annually and contains extended obituaries of deceased Fellows.{{cite web |url=http://rsbm.royalsocietypublishing.org/ |title=Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society |publisher=The Royal Society |access-date=11 December 2009 |archive-date=18 March 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110318100710/http://rsbm.royalsocietypublishing.org/ |url-status=live }} ''[[Open Biology]]'' is an [[open access journal]] covering [[biology]] at the [[Molecular biology|molecular]] and [[Cell biology|cellular level]]. ''[[Royal Society Open Science]]'' is an [[open access journal]] publishing high-quality original research across the entire range of science on the basis of objective peer-review.{{Cite web |url=http://rsos.royalsocietypublishing.org/ |title=ROYAL SOCIETY OPEN SCIENCE {{!}} Open Science |website=rsos.royalsocietypublishing.org |access-date=14 December 2016 |archive-date=1 December 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161201040917/http://rsos.royalsocietypublishing.org/ |url-status=live }} All the society's journals are [[Peer review|peer-reviewed]]. In May 2021, the society announced plans to transition its four [[Hybrid_open-access_journal|hybrid research journals]] to [[open access]].{{cite web |url=https://royalsociety.org/news/2021/05/royal-society-open-access-plans/ |title=The Royal Society sets 75% threshold to 'flip' its research journals to Open Access over the next five years |publisher=The Royal Society |access-date=3 June 2021 |date=13 May 2021 |archive-date=3 June 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210603095309/https://royalsociety.org/news/2021/05/royal-society-open-access-plans/ |url-status=live }} ==Honours== {{main|Awards, lectures and medals of the Royal Society}} The Royal Society presents numerous awards, lectures, and medals to recognise scientific achievement. The oldest is the [[Croonian Lecture]], created in 1701 at the request of the widow of [[William Croone]], one of the founding members of the Royal Society. The Croonian Lecture is still awarded on an annual basis and is considered the most important Royal Society prize for the biological sciences.{{cite web |url=https://royalsociety.org/grants-schemes-awards/awards/croonian-lecture/ |title=The Croonian Lecture (1738) |publisher=The Royal Society |access-date=7 February 2009 |archive-date=23 June 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200623104625/https://royalsociety.org/grants-schemes-awards/awards/croonian-lecture/ |url-status=live }} Although the Croonian Lecture was created in 1701, it was first awarded in 1738, seven years after the [[Copley Medal]]. The Copley Medal is the oldest Royal Society medal still in use and is awarded for "outstanding achievements in research in any branch of science".{{cite web
